title: Profiling and Debugging
learningGoals: Compare compiler vs interpreter, and explain why Python is both (bytecode .pyc + the Python Virtual Machine), plus JIT.
Distinguish compile time (static) vs run time (dynamic), and compile-time errors vs run-time errors (exceptions) vs logical errors.
Define profiling, explain static vs dynamic profiling, and read cProfile output (ncalls, tottime, percall, cumtime). Know pylint/radon (static) and memory profilers.
Define debugging. Use print/logging, then a debugger: breakpoints, watch, call stack, step over / step into / step out / continue, inspecting and setting variables. Know pdb.
sirStressed: Debugging is very, very important. Practise step over vs step into vs step out in VS Code. If you step over by mistake, you'll miss what happens inside the function.
A breakpoint pauses the program at run time; it doesn't stop it entirely. Then you watch the variables and the call stack.
Analogy: a teacher deducts marks because you subtracted instead of added. Logical errors like that happen in code too, and the debugger finds where.
"Just attending the classes is not at all sufficient." Experiment with the given programs and modify them, using AI tools if you like.
Assignment rules: AI tools are allowed for brainstorming, but never submit AI-generated or copied screenshots. That's easy to detect and costs marks. Use screenshots of your own real investigation.
commonTraps: Saying Python is only interpreted. Technically it's compiled to bytecode and then interpreted by the PVM.
Compile time = static; run time = dynamic. Don't swap them.
Treating divide-by-zero as a compile-time error. It's a run-time error (an exception).
Expecting a compiler or static profiler to measure time or memory. Only dynamic profiling can.
tottime vs cumtime: tottime excludes sub-calls; cumtime includes them.
Step out skips lines. Wrong: it executes them, just without pausing at each one.
Saying that a syntax error in Python still produces a .pyc . It doesn't.
summary: Compiler (C/C++): whole program → machine-code executable ahead of time. Fast. Interpreter: line by line, on demand, with no machine-code file. Flexible but slower. Python = compiled to bytecode (.pyc) + interpreted by the PVM (portable). JIT compiles hot code at run time.
Compile time = static (code as a file); run time = dynamic (the code is a running process).

Errors: compile-time (syntax: missing colon, wrong name; no bytecode), run-time / exceptions (divide by zero, missing file, memory full; the program stops at that line), logical (wrong output). Handle exceptions with try/except .

Profiling = where the time and resources go, to find bottlenecks. Profile first, then optimise. Static (pylint, radon): cyclomatic complexity, style, standards, comments, with no timing. Dynamic (cProfile + pstats, memory_profiler): time, calls, memory, spikes. Loops took 3.8 s vs NumPy 0.002 s.
cProfile columns: ncalls, tottime (self), percall, cumtime (including sub-calls).

Debugging = find + fix. Print/logging (the apartment-register analogy, log files) → debugger: breakpoint (pause), watch, call stack, step over (F10), step into (F11), step out, continue, inspect or set values.
Bugs seen: range(1,5) → use range(1,6) ; len(marks)-1 → use len(marks) .
pdb: b , c , n , s , r , p , l , w , q . gdb for C: break , run , next , step , finish , print , set var , x , bt .

questions.prompt: Just-in-time (JIT) compilation aims to:

options.text: Compile code at run time for faster execution

questions.explanation: JIT compiles the hot (frequently run) bytecode into machine code while the program runs.

questions.prompt: Which is TRUE about a compiler?

options.text: It converts one line at a time
It converts the entire source to machine code before execution

questions.explanation: converting the whole program ahead of time is the compiler's defining trait. Line by line is the interpreter.

questions.prompt: Which file extension stores Python bytecode?
questions.explanation: .pyc (stored in __pycache__ ). .class is Java bytecode.

questions.prompt: Static behaviour refers to:

options.text: Decisions made before the program runs

questions.explanation: static = compile time (the code as a file). Dynamic = run time (the running process).

options.text: Purely interpreted with no intermediate form

questions.explanation: cumtime includes sub-calls; tottime is the function's own time.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between static and dynamic profiling, with one tool each.
correctAnswers: Static analyses the source without running it: complexity, style, standards (for example pylint or radon), but no time or memory figures. Dynamic runs the program and measures time per function, call counts and memory (for example cProfile or memory_profiler).
questions.explanation: Static analyses the source without running it: complexity, style, standards (for example pylint or radon), but no time or memory figures. Dynamic runs the program and measures time per function, call counts and memory (for example cProfile or memory_profiler).

questions.prompt: Find the bug and fix it:
questions.code:
nums = [2, 4, 6]
s = 0
for i in range(1, len(nums)):
    s += nums[i]
print(s)   # expected 12
correctAnswers: The loop starts at index 1, which skips nums[0] = 2 , so it prints 10. Fix: for i in range(len(nums)): (or range(0, len(nums)) , or just s = sum(nums) ). The result is 12.
questions.explanation: The loop starts at index 1, which skips nums[0] = 2 , so it prints 10. Fix: for i in range(len(nums)): (or range(0, len(nums)) , or just s = sum(nums) ). The result is 12.

questions.prompt: Your data-pipeline script has become slow after new features were added. Describe the steps you'd take to fix it.
correctAnswers: (1) Profile first with python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py . (2) Look for the functions with high tottime/cumtime or huge ncalls, which are the hotspots. (3) Optimise those, for example by replacing Python loops with vectorised NumPy or pandas operations or removing repeated work. Check memory with memory_profiler. (4) Re-profile to confirm the improvement and that the output hasn't changed.
questions.explanation: (1) Profile first with python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py . (2) Look for the functions with high tottime/cumtime or huge ncalls, which are the hotspots. (3) Optimise those, for example by replacing Python loops with vectorised NumPy or pandas operations or removing repeated work. Check memory with memory_profiler. (4) Re-profile to confirm the improvement and that the output hasn't changed.

questions.prompt: Why is a debugger better than print statements for a 20,000-line program? Name 3 debugger features.
correctAnswers: Prints don't scale: you'd need thousands of them, editing and re-running each time. A debugger lets you pause anywhere (breakpoints), watch and inspect or change variables and memory, follow the call stack, and step over / into / out, localising the bug systematically without changing the code.
questions.explanation: Prints don't scale: you'd need thousands of them, editing and re-running each time. A debugger lets you pause anywhere (breakpoints), watch and inspect or change variables and memory, follow the call stack, and step over / into / out, localising the bug systematically without changing the code.
